title: Causal Discovery Voting Ensemble
one_liner: Use voting (like a jury) to combine multiple causal discovery guesses into one more reliable answer.
lead: Figuring out cause-and-effect from data is hard: each method makes different guesses depending on tiny changes to the data, and no method is always right. This paper treats multiple discovery methods like voters in an election and combines their votes mathematically to find the true causal graph. The voting rule comes with proof that it works.

problem.h2: Why a single causal discovery method fails
paras: Each causal discovery method (a tool that reads data and guesses which variables cause which) makes a different guess. Change the data slightly, or run the same method with different random starting points, and you get a different answer. The method might assume things about the data that are not true, or get stuck in a local optimum (a mediocre answer that is hard to escape from). A user cannot trust a single answer.

A naive approach: just pick the method that performed best on your past data and use that. But this fails because no method works everywhere — one that is great on data from biology might be terrible on data from economics.

callout.html: Single causal discovery methods give inconsistent answers; no one method works universally.

panels.title: 1. Many guesses
panels.caption: Three methods each guess a different cause-effect structure.

panels.title: 2. Inconsistency
panels.viz_args: Method A: B causes D. Method B: D causes B. Method C: unsure.
panels.caption: Same data, different answers. Which is right?

panels.title: 3. Voting
panels.caption: Count which edges (cause arrows) each method votes for most.

panels.title: 4. Weight the votes
panels.viz_args: Trust reliable voters more. Down-weight noisy ones.
panels.caption: Not all methods are equally accurate; give each a score.

panels.title: 5. One answer
panels.caption: Weighted votes produce one confident causal graph.

steps.text: Apply three or more different causal discovery algorithms to the data.
For each potential cause-arrow, count how many methods predict it exists.
Measure how often each method tends to be correct (its accuracy on test data).
Give high-accuracy methods larger voting power; ignore unreliable ones.
Include a cause-arrow only if weighted votes exceed a threshold.

paras: This paper changes how the ensemble combines predictions. Instead of heuristic (ad-hoc) averaging or majority vote, it uses mathematically justified weighted voting.
object.object: voting weights (how much each method's vote counts)

hidden.name: method competency (how accurate each method is)
paras: The paper identifies and measures one key hidden quantity: each method's true competency — how often that method correctly identifies real cause-and-effect edges. This is not just accuracy on all edges, but specifically how well that method ranks real edges higher than fake ones. The paper shows this competency score should determine each method's voting weight: a method with competency 0.8 (gets it right 80% of the time) votes with twice the power of a method with competency 0.6 (60% accurate).

The paper estimates competency from agreement patterns: if two very different methods both predict the same edge, that edge is more likely to be real, so both methods gained evidence they are competent on this data.

heat.caption: Darker shades show higher competency scores; top methods (A, C, E, G, I, K) vote more.

reads.html: A method that gets 8 out of 10 causal relationships right is more trustworthy than one that gets 4 out of 10, so we listen to it more.

The paper derives that optimal voting weights are proportional to a method's accuracy in recovering the true directed acyclic graph (DAG), with theoretical guarantees that this weighting recovers the ground truth under certain conditions.

mechanism.h2: Why weighted voting recovers the true causal graph
paras: Here is why it works: if you run many methods and weight their votes by accuracy, accurate methods will outvote the inaccurate ones. An accurate method correctly predicts most real cause-arrows and correctly rejects most false ones. An inaccurate method predicts randomly, so its votes scatter. When you take a weighted sum, the accurate methods' votes all point in the same true direction, but the inaccurate methods' votes cancel out. The final vote count is dominated by truth.

The paper proves this formally: under certain conditions (the methods must be independent, i.e., not all making the same systematic mistake, and the true causal graph must be identifiable from the data), the weighted voting ensemble recovers the true graph with high probability. The weights are set using the competency scores. If you use equal weights instead, you lose this guarantee — inaccurate methods drag down the answer.

stages.s: weighted vote: multiply each edge count by method weight
threshold: include edges above the vote cutoff

math.words: Total vote for edge (i to j) equals sum of each method's competency times its prediction of that edge
symbols: total weighted votes for cause-arrow from i to j
1 if method k predicts edge i→j, 0 if not
index over all methods in the ensemble

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Three methods run on a dataset with variables A, B, C.
Method-1: competency 0.9 (very accurate); predicts edges A→B and A→C.
Method-2: competency 0.6 (medium); predicts edges A→B and B→C.
Method-3: competency 0.3 (weak); predicts B→A and B→C.
If threshold is 1.0: A→B wins (1.5≥1), others lose.
Result: A causes B (only edge above threshold). Accurate.

math.note: Trustworthy methods (high weights) tip the vote toward truth; noisy methods contribute less.

charts.title: Single best method
charts.note: One method excels in one setting but fails when data is noisy or from a different domain.

charts.title: Weighted voting ensemble
charts.note: The ensemble drops less when conditions change because multiple methods average out each one's blind spots.

items.b: All methods fail the same way.
items.html: If every method makes the same systematic mistake (e.g., all assume there are no cycles in the cause-graph when there actually are), weighted voting will not help because all votes point in the same wrong direction, so the weighted sum is still wrong. The paper's math assumes the methods are independent — each one's errors are different, so they cancel out. This breaks if all methods share a blind spot.
If every method is a small tweak of one base algorithm, they all inherit the same flaw. Voting only works if methods are truly independent.
If you measure each method's accuracy on a small or non-representative test set, the weights will be unreliable, and the ensemble can be worse than a naive average.
Use diverse methods (different algorithm families); estimate competency on a held-out test set; ensure the true causal graph is identifiable from the data you have.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a synthetic causal system where you know the true graph (e.g., a small acyclic graph where variable A causes B and C, and B causes C). Run three causal discovery methods on this data. Measure each method's accuracy (true positives and true negatives for edges). Build a voting ensemble with weights set by those accuracies. Compare the ensemble's graph against the ground truth; also compare it to (1) each single method alone and (2) an unweighted ensemble (equal vote for each method). The demo should show that weighted voting finds more edges correctly than any single method or unweighted ensemble, especially when data is noisy.
demo.metric_eq: accuracy = (true edges found + true non-edges rejected) / total possible edges
demo.closing: Weighted voting should recover the true causal structure with fewer false alarms than any single method, even on noisy data.
